summary: NASA explains our planet with colourful maps, but a colour bar means nothing to someone who cannot see it. The Earth Information Jukebox turns real NASA images into music that describes them, so blind and low-vision people, and anyone who learns by listening, can explore Earth science by ear. Our engine first reads what each colour means using NASA’s own colour bar or legend. A line then sweeps the picture from west to east in 8 seconds, and the sound moves from your left ear to your right. Each region or kind of particle gets its own instrument, all notes stay on one pentatonic scale so it always sounds musical, and where there is nothing to report there is silence, so on the ocean map you can hear the shape of the continents. We built three tracks from NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio: ocean surface temperature, aerosols on 19 August 2025, and lightning seen from the International Space Station. Click any spot, or use the arrow keys, to hear its note and have the place name and value read aloud, for example “Arabian Sea, 29.4 °C”. Accessible mode gives full keyboard control, speech and high contrast, and users can upload their own colour maps too. The temperatures our engine reads from the ocean image (28.4 °C at the equator, 2.5 °C near 60° south) follow the real ocean pattern, and all 28 automated checks pass.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

The Earth Information Jukebox turns real NASA images of Earth into music that describes them, so blind and low-vision people, and anyone who learns by listening, can explore Earth science by ear.

1. Read the meaning of the colours. Before making any sound, our engine works out what each colour stands for, using NASA's own colour bar or legend. On the ocean map, colours become temperatures from 0 to 32 °C. On the aerosol map, colours become sulfate, dust, smoke and sea salt. On the lightning map, yellow dots become flashes. For an image someone uploads, the engine learns the colour scale from the picture itself.

2. Sweep the picture. A line moves across the picture from left to right (west to east) in 8 seconds, and the sound moves from your left ear to your right ear with it.

3. Give each part its own instrument. On the ocean map, the northern oceans play the marimba, the tropics play the strings and the southern oceans play plucked notes. On the aerosol map, dust plays the strings, smoke the bell, sulfate the marimba and sea salt the flute. Never more than three sounds play at once, so the listener can follow them.

4. Turn values into notes. Warmer water plays higher notes. All notes stay on one pentatonic scale, so it always sounds musical.

5. Use silence as information. Where there is no data, there is no sound, so on the ocean map you can hear the shape of the continents.

Explore any spot: click or drag on the picture, or use the arrow keys, to hear the note at that spot and have the place name and value read aloud. For example: "Arabian Sea, 29.4 °C", "Maharashtra, India, this is land", or "Kasai-Occidental, Democratic Republic of the Congo, lightning here". Place names cover every state, province, ocean and sea in the world.

Two modes: Standard mode
dataRefs: NASA SVS 3912: Global Sea Surface Currents and Temperature (ECCO2)
NASA SVS 5011: Lightning seen by the ISS Lightning Imaging Sensor
projectRefs: Natural Earth: states, provinces and seas (place names, public domain)
Natural Earth vector files (source of the place-name data)
Web Audio API (explore sounds in the browser)

Claude by Anthropic (AI assistant: code, slides, documents)
